{{User page}}

Detailed method for [[../|the Bay Area 2026 elections proposal]]. This page is
the "how"; the parent page is the "what and why", and is where discussion should
happen.

Written for one region and one cycle, but deliberately not specific to either —
the structure applies anywhere an elections authority publishes certified
results.

== Scope ==

Two gates, applied in order.

=== The office-class floor ===

'''In scope:''' federal, state legislative, county offices, and major-city
offices. '''Out of scope:''' school boards, special districts, and municipal
offices below the major-city line. Statewide offices are also out, as not
specific to the region.

This is an editorial judgment, not a derived one. The intent is to stop well
above the point where a candidate stops being a public figure in any meaningful
sense. Someone standing for Congress, a county board, or a city council in a
substantial city has sought public office and public scrutiny; a first-time
candidate for a minor local body has not, to the same degree.

That line should not be decidable by the accident of whether someone happens to
have a Wikidata item, which is what would happen if the mechanical gate below
were the only control.

'''"Major city" means population ≥ 100,000, or the seat of one of the nine
counties''' — both checkable via {{P|P1082}} and {{P|P36}}, so the line is
chosen editorially but applied mechanically. That gives sixteen cities over the
population line plus four county seats below it. San Francisco is handled as a
county, being a consolidated city-county.

Charter-city status was considered as the line and rejected: it is close to
uncorrelated with significance, excluding Fremont, Hayward and Daly City while
admitting cities of around ten thousand people, and it changes by ballot measure
for unrelated fiscal reasons.

=== The mechanical bar ===

Among contests passing the floor, a contest is included if '''either''' enwiki
has an article for it, '''or''' at least one certified candidate has a Wikidata
item. Both are checkable, and both are evidence that someone independent of this
project already judged the subject notable.

This applies to district contests too, which is why there is no vote-share
threshold: a district is in scope if any of its counties is a Bay Area county.
Share of a district's electorate does not measure whether an office represents
Bay Area constituents — one Assembly district is 18% Santa Clara and is held by
the Speaker of the California State Assembly.

== Step 1: build a register of contests ==

An auditable inventory of every in-scope contest, with the source establishing
each one, published as a subpage of the parent.

=== Re-discovered each cycle, never carried forward ===

The register makes the next cycle cheaper, but it is rebuilt from sources rather
than diffed. Contests appear and disappear for reasons no diff predicts:
voting-rights settlements convert cities from at-large to district elections,
creating seats that did not previously exist — over 600 California local bodies
since 2002, on litigation timelines — and boundaries move mid-decade, as
California's congressional districts did by ballot measure in November 2025.

=== Federal and state legislative ===

The state's certified results publication covers every congressional and
legislative contest, one workbook per office class (see [[#Sources|Sources]]).
Each district block lists per-county vote totals, so regional membership is
derived from the documents themselves rather than from a maintained list of
districts.

Under California's top-two rule the two highest vote-getters advance, so for
this tier one document is simultaneously the contest list, the candidate list,
and the reference.

Measured 2026-07-31: 34 districts touch the Bay Area, yielding 67 advancing
candidates — 32 resolving confidently to Wikidata items, 9 ambiguous, 26 with no
item.

=== County and municipal contests ===

There is no state-level aggregation; each county publishes independently, and
formats differ. For each county, work down until a source is found: the county
elections office; the county clerk where elections sit there; the state's
published directory of county elections officials, which is the reliable way to
find an office whose website has moved; then direct contact.

A source is usable when it is '''published by the elections official''' — not a
news outlet or aggregator — is dated, and enumerates the November ballot for
that contest. Ballotpedia, news coverage and candidate websites may be used to
''find'' a contest; they are never the reference on the resulting statement.

Capture the URL, the retrieval date, and an archive snapshot, because county
pages are reorganised aggressively after each election and a reference that
404s in two years cannot be checked.

'''Where a source is missing, record that fact rather than skipping the
county.''' A county with no usable source should be a visible gap, not an
apparent absence of contests. Several county sites resist automated access; that
is a property of the sources, and this tier is partly manual by nature.

Note that most municipal contests have '''no primary''', and several Bay Area
cities use ranked-choice voting, so every certified candidate appears on the
November ballot rather than a top two. Expect more candidates per contest here
than in the district tier, and a larger proportion with no Wikidata item.

== Step 2: election items and their data model ==

=== Where the model comes from ===

For congressional and legislative contests the previous cycle's item is a good
model: it already carries date, jurisdiction, office contested and series links,
so the argument is simply that this cycle should match the last one.

For local contests the previous cycle is '''not''' a usable model. The 2024 Bay
Area local election items carry only {{P|P31}}, sometimes {{P|P17}} — one adds
{{P|P1001}}. The model here is instead taken from better-developed mayoral items
elsewhere: {{Q|Q85737931}}, {{Q|Q118966754}} and the Boston, Chicago and Los
Angeles equivalents, which are consistent with each other.

Whether that is the right template — and whether it should be formalised as an
[[Wikidata:Schemas|EntitySchema]] — is one of the open questions on the parent
page.

=== Proposed properties ===

For contests whose election item covers the whole state:

{| class="wikitable"
! Property !! Value
|-
| {{P|P585}} || the general-election date
|-
| {{P|P1001}} || the state
|-
| {{P|P541}} || the office contested
|-
| {{P|P361}} || the national or statewide parent
|-
| {{P|P155}} || the previous cycle's equivalent
|}

For contests whose election item covers a single county or city:

{| class="wikitable"
! Property !! Value
|-
| {{P|P585}} || the general-election date
|-
| {{P|P1001}} || the county or city
|-
| {{P|P541}} || the office contested
|-
| {{P|P31}} || the election-series class where one exists, else {{Q|Q40231}}
|-
| {{P|P155}} / {{P|P156}} || the adjacent cycles
|}

{{P|P991}} is out of scope until after the election.

{{P|P1001}} is the load-bearing one for local items: it is what makes them
discoverable geographically, with no list of QIDs maintained anywhere. Contests
whose item is statewide cannot work this way, since district items are modelled
{{P|P131}} → the state rather than → county — which is the subject of one of the
open questions.

=== Creating items ===

Create only where the register entry has a source. Before creating, search for
an existing item under variant names: '''name-pattern search is a starting
point, not a check''', since it misses items filed under other names and returns
confident false matches from elsewhere in the world — place names repeat across
countries. Confirm by jurisdiction and date, never by label.

'''Naming.''' There is no single established pattern — existing items use
adjectival forms, office-name forms, and plural county omnibus forms. So: mirror
the enwiki article title where one exists; otherwise mirror the previous cycle's
item for the same jurisdiction and office; never invent a third form for a
jurisdiction that already has one.

'''Notability.''' [[Wikidata:Notability]] criterion 2 appears to cover these: a
certified election for a named public office, documented by an official canvass
published by the responsible elections authority, is a clearly identifiable
entity with public references. Criterion 3 arguably also applies, but criterion 2
is the better argument — a structural need created by one's own project is a
weaker claim.

=== Checking completeness ===

One query over the register returns one row per '''missing''' required property.
An empty result means every item is complete; because the query is generated
from the register, re-running it re-checks everything, including items fixed in
earlier passes.

{{SPARQL|query=SELECT ?item ?itemLabel ?missingLabel WHERE {
  VALUES (?item ?missing) {
    (wd:Q131470954 wd:P585) (wd:Q131470954 wd:P1001) (wd:Q131470954 wd:P541)
    (wd:Q131470954 wd:P361) (wd:Q131470954 wd:P155)
    (wd:Q138112703 wd:P585) (wd:Q138112703 wd:P1001) (wd:Q138112703 wd:P541)
  }
  ?missing wikibase:directClaim ?dc .
  FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?item ?dc [] }
  SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". }
}
ORDER BY ?itemLabel}}

Binding the property as an entity and dereferencing <code>wikibase:directClaim</code>
is what lets one query check different requirements per class without
enumerating them in code. Run as shown, {{Q|Q131470954}} returns nothing and
{{Q|Q138112703}} returns three rows.

== Step 3: candidates ==

=== Names cannot be matched on names ===

Matching a candidate's name against labels fails in two ways that are common
rather than exotic, and it fails ''confidently''.

Disambiguation items carry the plain name as their label, so a name matches both
the disambiguation item and the person with nothing in the label to separate
them. And namesakes are ordinary: Bay Area candidates this cycle share exact
names with an actor who died in 2002, a cricketer born in 1868, and a film
producer.

So: '''never accept a name→QID match on a label.''' Require {{P|P31}} =
{{Q|Q5}} as a hard gate, rank on corroborating evidence, and treat a close
second place as a reason for review rather than a tiebreak to resolve
automatically.

=== Scoring ===

Candidates are scored on {{P|P106}} = politician, holding any {{P|P39}},
{{P|P27}} = United States, and having an enwiki sitelink. Items failing
{{P|P31}} = {{Q|Q5}} are discarded rather than ranked. A match is treated as
confident only if it scores well '''and''' strictly beats the runner-up.

Results fall into three tiers, and '''none of them writes directly''':

* '''Confident''' — generates a batch for review.
* '''Ambiguous''' — generates a list showing each rival item and its
  description, so a human can see what the match was chosen over.
* '''No item''' — recorded as a coverage gap. Not a worklist for creating items;
  see the parent page.

The confident tier is reviewed rather than trusted. The score measures whether
an item is a plausible American public figure, not whether it is the person who
stood in this contest — a long-dead labour leader satisfies every signal.

=== Statement direction ===

Working assumption, and '''the least settled part of this method''':
{{P|P3602}} on the person qualified with {{P|P768}} for congressional and
legislative contests, since there is no per-district election item to attach
{{P|P726}} to; {{P|P726}} on the election item for mayoral and council contests.
This is inferred from a handful of items and is an open question on the parent
page.

=== References ===

Every candidacy statement carries {{P|P854}}, {{P|P1476}} and {{P|P813}}, plus
{{P|P577}} only where the source states a publication date — never inferred from
statutory deadlines.

The test a source must pass:

: '''The source must establish who is on the November ballot''' — not merely who
filed, and not merely who exists.

For contests with a primary, the certified results establish who advanced; a
pre-primary filing list does not. For contests whose first round is November,
the general-election certified candidate list does establish it, because it
enumerates exactly the people on that ballot. The test is on what a document
''establishes'', never on what it is called — a blanket rule against filing
lists would make every no-primary contest permanently unlinkable.

{{P|P143}} is not used, for the reason given on the parent page.

=== Batch hygiene ===

A removal takes no qualifiers, or QuickStatements splits the line into a
malformed second command. QuickStatements also decomposes one input line into
several commands — statement, qualifiers, references — so a summary reporting
errors must be read per row.

Neither a batch summary nor the absence of errors is evidence of correctness.
'''The verification query is''', and every batch is paired with the query that
checks it.

== Review ==

Per proposed candidacy statement, before the batch runs:

# The target item is {{P|P31}} = {{Q|Q5}} — not a disambiguation item, not an
  organisation.
# Its description, occupation or held positions are consistent with a 2026
  candidate for this office.
# It is not a different person of the same name — check dates of birth and
  death, nationality, and the enwiki article where one exists.
# The cited source actually names this person for this contest. Open it.
# The qualifier district or jurisdiction matches the source.

Per election-item statement: the item is the right election, the jurisdiction
and office are correct, and the date is the general-election date.

How much of this should remain manual is an open question on the parent page.
The stages differ enormously in risk: parsing certified results, writing
data-model statements from a fixed template, and attaching references are
ordinary data processing, while resolving a name to a QID is the stage with a
measured error rate and living-person exposure.
